did_you_know.text: Did you know? The title presents the psalm as “A Prayer of the Afflicted”—a prayer from someone in distress who seeks to pour out his complaint before the Lord.
Did you know? The psalmist describes his days as fading away like smoke and his bones as burning, expressing profound weakness and pain.
Did you know? His sense of loneliness is conveyed through images of birds: the psalmist compares himself to a desert owl and an owl among the ruins.
Did you know? The phrase “like a solitary bird on a roof” emphasizes the worshiper’s watchfulness and loneliness as he remains alone through the night.
Did you know? In contrast to the fleeting days of human life, the psalmist sets the Lord, who endures forever, and whose name is remembered from generation to generation.
Did you know? The plea for mercy on Zion is linked in the psalm to the “appointed time”—the time set for compassion and mercy to be shown to her.
Did you know? The psalm emphasizes that the Lord responds to the prayer of the afflicted and does not despise it; thus, the prayer of distress becomes a central part of hope.
Did you know? The purpose of deliverance is not merely personal: it is meant to proclaim the Lord’s name and praise in Zion and Jerusalem.
Did you know? The psalm’s vision includes peoples and kingdoms gathering together to serve the Lord, so its hope is both universal and national in scope.

Did you know? The earth and the heavens are described as the work of the Lord’s hands, while they themselves will one day change and perish; this highlights the Lord’s everlasting nature in contrast to them.
